units.title: Symbols and Translation
units.blurb: Statements as letters joined by five connectives (¬ ∧ ∨ → ↔): reading formulas, finding the main connective, and translating English to symbols and back.

units.title: Truth Tables
units.blurb: Truth values, full truth tables, tautologies and equivalences, and deciding validity by a full table or a short one.

units.title: Natural Deduction: Rules of Inference
units.blurb: Formal proofs line by line with the eight rules of inference: MP, MT, HS, DS, CD, Simp, Conj and Add.

units.title: Rules of Replacement
units.blurb: Equivalences that can rewrite any part of a line: DN, DM, Com, Assoc, Dist, Trans, Impl, Equiv, Exp and Taut.

units.title: Conditional and Indirect Proof
units.blurb: Proofs with assumptions: conditional proof (CP), indirect proof (IP), and nested subproofs, which can prove theorems from no premises at all.

units.title: Predicate Logic: Translation and Truth
units.blurb: Inside the statement: predicates, names and quantifiers (∀ ∃), translating categorical and harder sentences, quantifier negation, and truth in a small world.

units.title: Predicate Logic: Proofs
units.blurb: The four quantifier rules (UI, EI, UG, EG) and their restrictions, and proofs that use them with CP, IP and QN.

units.title: Relations and Identity
units.blurb: Predicates of two or more places, the order of quantifiers, properties of relations, and identity for "only", "at least", "at most" and "exactly".

units.title: Soundness and Completeness
units.blurb: Stepping back: the difference between provable and valid, and why a good proof system is both sound and complete.

topics.title: Simple and Compound Statements
topics.short: A simple statement has no other statement as a part; a compound statement is built from simpler ones with words like not, and, or, if.
topics.trouble: Learners call "Ann and Ben are cousins" compound. It does not say "Ann is a cousin and Ben is a cousin"; it states one relation, so it is simple.

topics.title: The Five Connectives
topics.short: Negation ¬, conjunction ∧, disjunction ∨, conditional → and biconditional ↔ build compound formulas from statement letters.
topics.trouble: Learners read ∨ as "one or the other but not both". In logic, p ∨ q is true when either or both are true.

topics.title: The Main Connective and Scope
topics.short: Parentheses group a formula; the main connective is the one with the widest scope, applied last, and it decides what kind of statement the formula is.
topics.trouble: The scope of negation: ¬p ∧ q negates only p, while ¬(p ∧ q) negates the whole conjunction. Learners drop the parentheses and change the meaning.

topics.title: Translating Not, And and Or
topics.short: "But", "although" and "yet" are ∧; "neither p nor q" is ¬(p ∨ q) or ¬p ∧ ¬q; "not both" is ¬(p ∧ q).
topics.trouble: Learners write "neither p nor q" as ¬p ∨ ¬q, which means "not both". Neither-nor denies each one.

topics.title: Translating Conditionals
topics.short: "If p, q", "q if p", "p only if q", "q provided that p", "p is sufficient for q" and "q is necessary for p" are all p → q; "p unless q" is ¬q → p, or p ∨ q.
topics.trouble: "Only if" reversed, and "necessary" mixed up with "sufficient": "You pass only if you study" is pass → study, not study → pass.

topics.title: Biconditionals and Longer Sentences
topics.short: "p if and only if q" and "p just in case q" are p ↔ q; longer sentences are translated from the main connective inward.
topics.trouble: Learners translate word by word from left to right. Find the main connective in the English first; commas and "either" often mark the grouping.

topics.title: From Symbols Back to English
topics.short: Read a formula aloud in plain English that keeps its grouping, using "either…or", "both…and" and "it is not the case that".
topics.trouble: Learners read ¬(p ∧ q) as "not p and not q". Phrases like "not both" keep the scope of the negation clear.

topics.title: Truth Values of the Connectives
topics.short: Each connective is a truth function: the truth value of the compound depends only on the values of its parts.
topics.trouble: The conditional with a false antecedent: learners call p → q false or "not applicable" when p is false. It is true; the promise was not broken.

topics.title: Computing a Truth Value
topics.short: Given the values of the letters, work from the innermost parts outward to find the value of the whole formula.
topics.trouble: Learners work left to right instead of from the inside out, or apply a negation to the wrong part.

topics.title: Building a Truth Table
topics.short: A formula with n letters has 2ⁿ rows; list them in a fixed order and fill a column for each part, ending with the main connective.
topics.trouble: Learners miss rows or repeat them. Halve the pattern for each letter: T T F F, then T F T F.

topics.title: Tautologies, Contradictions and Contingent Statements
topics.short: A tautology is true in every row, a self-contradiction false in every row, and a contingent statement true in some rows and false in others.
topics.trouble: Learners call a statement a tautology after checking a few rows. Every row must be checked; one F makes it not a tautology.

topics.title: Logical Equivalence
topics.short: Two formulas are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value in every row; then their biconditional is a tautology.
topics.trouble: Learners compare only the rows where a formula is true, or decide two formulas are equivalent because they look alike.

topics.title: De Morgan's Laws
topics.short: ¬(p ∧ q) is equivalent to ¬p ∨ ¬q, and ¬(p ∨ q) to ¬p ∧ ¬q: moving a negation inside flips ∧ and ∨.
topics.trouble: The scope of negation: learners distribute the ¬ but keep the same connective, writing ¬(p ∧ q) as ¬p ∧ ¬q.

topics.title: Converse, Inverse and Contrapositive
topics.short: p → q is equivalent to its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p, but not to its converse q → p or its inverse ¬p → ¬q.
topics.trouble: Treating the converse as equivalent is affirming the consequent in disguise. A truth table shows the row where they differ.

topics.title: Consistent, Inconsistent and Contradictory
topics.short: Statements are consistent if some row makes them all true; two statements are contradictory if they have opposite values in every row.
topics.trouble: Learners call any two statements that disagree "contradictory". Inconsistent statements cannot all be true, but, unlike contradictories, they may all be false.

topics.title: Validity by Truth Table
topics.short: An argument is valid when no row makes every premise true and the conclusion false.
topics.trouble: Learners look for a row where everything is true and call the argument valid, or call it invalid because some row has a false premise.

topics.title: The Short Truth Table Method
topics.short: Assume the premises true and the conclusion false, then work out the forced values; if that leads to a contradiction, the argument is valid.
topics.trouble: Learners stop at the first forced value, or call the argument invalid when they were the ones who made a mistake. Every value must be forced or tried both ways.

topics.title: Valid and Invalid Argument Forms
topics.short: Modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical and disjunctive syllogism are valid forms; affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are invalid.
topics.trouble: Affirming the consequent looks like modus ponens. Check which part of the conditional the second premise matches.

topics.title: What a Formal Proof Is
topics.short: A proof is a numbered list of lines; each is a premise or follows from earlier lines by a rule, written beside it with the line numbers it uses.
topics.trouble: Learners think a proof must use every premise or must be the shortest one. Any correct chain of justified lines that ends in the conclusion is a proof.

topics.title: Modus Ponens and Modus Tollens (MP, MT)
topics.short: MP: from p → q and p, infer q. MT: from p → q and ¬q, infer ¬p. The letters can stand for any formulas.
topics.trouble: Learners apply MP with the consequent instead of the antecedent (affirming the consequent), or apply MT to ¬p instead of ¬q.

topics.title: Hypothetical and Disjunctive Syllogism (HS, DS)
topics.short: HS: from p → q and q → r, infer p → r. DS: from p ∨ q and ¬p, infer q.
topics.trouble: Learners use DS with an affirmed disjunct (p ∨ q and p, so ¬q), which is invalid since "or" is inclusive.

topics.title: Simplification, Conjunction and Addition (Simp, Conj, Add)
topics.short: Simp: from p ∧ q, infer p. Conj: from p and q, infer p ∧ q. Add: from p, infer p ∨ q for any q at all.
topics.trouble: Addition feels like cheating, and learners wrongly apply Simp to a disjunction. From p ∨ q you cannot infer p.

topics.title: Constructive Dilemma (CD)
topics.short: CD: from (p → q) ∧ (r → s) and p ∨ r, infer q ∨ s.
topics.trouble: Learners use CD with the two conditionals on separate lines. In this system the conditionals must be joined in one conjunction first (Conj).

topics.title: Matching a Rule to Whole Lines
topics.short: A rule of inference applies only to whole lines whose main connectives match the rule's pattern, with any formulas in place of p, q, r and s.
topics.trouble: Learners apply MP inside a line: from (p → q) ∨ r and p they infer q. Rules of inference never work on a part of a line.

topics.title: Justifying Proof Lines
topics.short: Name the rule and the earlier lines that justify each line of a finished proof.
topics.trouble: Learners cite the right rule with the wrong lines, or cite lines that come after the one being justified.

topics.title: Building Short Proofs
topics.short: Supply the missing lines of short proofs, choosing each step by what the conclusion needs.
topics.trouble: Learners write down every line they can infer and get lost. Start from the conclusion and ask which rule could produce it.

topics.title: Proof Strategy: Working Backward
topics.short: Find the conclusion inside the premises, then plan which rule would produce it and what that rule needs.
topics.trouble: Learners never use Add, because it seems to lose information. When a letter in the conclusion appears in no premise, Add is usually how it gets in.

topics.title: Rules of Replacement
topics.short: A replacement rule says two forms are equivalent, so either can replace the other anywhere, even inside a line, in either direction.
topics.trouble: Learners treat replacement rules like inference rules and use them only on whole lines, or treat inference rules like replacement rules and use them on parts.

topics.title: De Morgan and Double Negation (DM, DN)
topics.trouble: The scope of negation again: ¬(p ∨ q) is not ¬p ∨ ¬q. DM moves the negation inside and changes the connective.

topics.title: Commutation, Association and Distribution (Com, Assoc, Dist)
topics.short: Com swaps the sides of ∧ or ∨; Assoc regroups three parts joined by the same connective; Dist spreads ∧ over ∨ and ∨ over ∧.
topics.trouble: Learners use Com on a conditional (p → q into q → p) or Assoc on mixed connectives. Neither is allowed.

topics.title: Transposition and Material Implication (Trans, Impl)
topics.short: Trans: p → q :: ¬q → ¬p. Impl: p → q :: ¬p ∨ q.
topics.trouble: Learners transpose without negating both sides, or write Impl as p ∨ ¬q.

topics.title: Equivalence, Exportation and Tautology (Equiv, Exp, Taut)
topics.short: Equiv: p ↔ q :: (p → q) ∧ (q → p), or (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ ¬q). Exp: (p ∧ q) → r :: p → (q → r). Taut: p :: p ∧ p and p :: p ∨ p.
topics.trouble: Learners export into (p → q) → r, which is not equivalent. Exportation moves the first conjunct out in front.

topics.title: Proofs with All Eighteen Rules
topics.short: Combine rules of inference and replacement, often reshaping a line with replacement until an inference rule fits.
topics.trouble: Learners reach for a long chain of replacements when a short inference would do. Ask what shape of line the next inference rule needs.

topics.title: Conditional Proof (CP)
topics.short: To prove p → q, assume p, derive q inside an indented subproof, then close it and write p → q.
topics.trouble: Learners use a line from inside a closed subproof later on. Once the subproof is closed, its lines depended on an assumption and cannot be cited.

topics.title: Indirect Proof (IP)
topics.short: To prove p, assume ¬p, derive a contradiction q ∧ ¬q, then close the subproof and write p.
topics.trouble: Learners stop when they reach some false-looking line. The subproof must reach an explicit contradiction of the form q ∧ ¬q.

topics.title: Nested Subproofs
topics.short: Subproofs can sit inside other subproofs; each must be closed, innermost first, and a theorem can be proved this way from no premises at all.
topics.trouble: Learners close the outer subproof before the inner one, or end the proof with a subproof still open.

topics.title: Predicates and Names
topics.short: A predicate letter stands for a property (F: is friendly) and a lowercase name for an individual (a: Ava); Fa says that Ava is friendly.
topics.trouble: Learners write the name first (aF) or use a capital letter for an individual. Predicate first, then name: Fa.

topics.title: The Quantifiers ∀ and ∃
topics.short: ∀x Fx says everything is F; ∃x Fx says at least one thing is F. A variable is bound when a quantifier covers it.
topics.trouble: "Some" read as "some but not all": ∃x Fx stays true when everything is F.

topics.title: Translating A, E, I and O
topics.short: A: ∀x(Sx → Px). E: ∀x(Sx → ¬Px). I: ∃x(Sx ∧ Px). O: ∃x(Sx ∧ ¬Px).
topics.trouble: Learners pair ∀ with ∧ or ∃ with →. ∀x(Sx ∧ Px) says everything is both S and P, and ∃x(Sx → Px) is true if anything at all is not S.

topics.title: Translating Harder Quantified Sentences
topics.short: Handle "only", "none but", "all except", complex subjects (red cars) and complex predicates (fast or loud) inside one quantifier.
topics.trouble: Learners translate "Only S are P" as ∀x(Sx → Px). It is ∀x(Px → Sx): everything that is P is S.

topics.title: Quantifier Negation
topics.short: ¬∀x Fx is equivalent to ∃x ¬Fx, and ¬∃x Fx to ∀x ¬Fx: moving a negation across a quantifier flips ∀ and ∃.
topics.trouble: The scope of negation: learners write ¬∀x Fx as ∀x ¬Fx ("not everything is F" is not "nothing is F").

topics.title: Truth in a Small World
topics.short: In a world with a few named objects, ∀x Fx is true when every object is F, and ∃x Fx when at least one is.
topics.trouble: Learners think ∀x(Fx → Gx) is false in a world with no F at all. With no F to break it, it is true.

topics.title: Counterexample Worlds
topics.short: Show an argument invalid by describing a small world where all its premises are true and its conclusion false.
topics.trouble: Learners build a world where the conclusion is false but forget to check that every premise is still true in it.

topics.title: Universal Instantiation and Existential Generalization (UI, EG)
topics.short: UI: from ∀x Fx, infer Fa for any name. EG: from Fa, infer ∃x Fx.
topics.trouble: Learners apply UI to part of a line, such as ∀x Fx → Ga. Like rules of inference, the quantifier rules act only on whole lines.

topics.title: Existential Instantiation (EI)
topics.short: EI: from ∃x Fx, infer Fa only for a name a that is new: not in any earlier line, the premises or the conclusion.
topics.trouble: Reusing a name: from ∃x Fx and ∃x Gx, learners write Fa and then Ga, as if the same thing had both properties.

topics.title: Universal Generalization (UG)
topics.short: UG: from Fy, infer ∀x Fx only when y is a variable standing for any object, not a name and not one introduced by EI.
topics.trouble: Learners generalize from a particular name: from Fa they write ∀x Fx. Showing one object is F does not show every object is.

topics.title: Proofs with Quantifiers
topics.short: Strip the quantifiers (EI before UI), reason with the propositional rules, then put quantifiers back with UG or EG.
topics.trouble: Learners use UI first and then cannot use EI with a new name. Do EI first when both are needed.

topics.title: Conditional and Indirect Proof with Quantifiers
topics.short: CP, IP and quantifier negation (QN) work in predicate logic too, as long as each quantifier rule's restrictions are kept.
topics.trouble: Learners use UG inside a subproof on a variable that appears free in the assumption, which proves too much.

topics.title: Relational Predicates
topics.short: A relational predicate links two or more objects in order: Lab says a likes b, which is not the same as Lba.
topics.trouble: Learners ignore the order of the names. "Ava helps Ben" and "Ben helps Ava" are different claims.

topics.title: Quantifier Order
topics.short: ∀x∃y Lxy (everyone likes someone) differs from ∃y∀x Lxy (someone is liked by everyone); the order of mixed quantifiers matters.
topics.trouble: Quantifier order: learners treat ∀x∃y and ∃y∀x as the same. The first lets each x pick its own y; the second needs one y for all.

topics.title: Properties of Relations
topics.short: A relation can be reflexive (Rxx for all x), symmetric (Rxy → Ryx) and transitive (Rxy ∧ Ryz → Rxz), or fail any of them.
topics.trouble: Learners think a relation that is not symmetric must be asymmetric. "Loves" can hold both ways for some pairs and one way for others.

topics.title: Identity
topics.short: a = b says a and b are the same object; identity lets us say "only", "someone other than" and "the same".
topics.trouble: Learners read a = b as "a and b are alike". Identity means one object with two names.

topics.title: At Least, At Most and Exactly
topics.short: With identity we can count: "at least two F" is ∃x∃y(Fx ∧ Fy ∧ x ≠ y); "at most one" and "exactly one" follow the same pattern.
topics.trouble: Learners write ∃x∃y(Fx ∧ Fy) for "at least two". Without x ≠ y, x and y can be the same object.

topics.title: Proofs with Identity
topics.short: The identity rules: a = a may be written anywhere, a = b gives b = a, and from Fa and a = b infer Fb.
topics.trouble: Learners substitute in the wrong direction or treat "a = b" as a premise about a property.

topics.title: Soundness and Completeness
topics.short: Provable (⊢) is about rules; valid (⊨) is about truth. A system is sound if everything provable is valid, and complete if everything valid is provable; our rules are both.
topics.trouble: Learners swap the two. Soundness: the rules never prove an invalid argument. Completeness: the rules can prove every valid one.
